newsitem.title: UK: UK builders, unions hold talks to avert strikes.
newsitem.headline: UK builders, unions hold talks to avert strikes.

text.p: Union leaders representing 40,000 British building workers and their main employers group will hold talks later on Thursday in a bid to settle a pay dispute which threatens to spark walkouts at key construction sites, a union official said.
Strikes by disgruntled workers could hit high-profile construction contracts worth hundreds of millions of pounds (dollars) to the industry.

The unions have pencilled in walkouts next month at prestigious projects such as the costly extension to the London Underground's Jubilee Line and work on the state-funded Millennium Dome, the GMB official said.
The pay talks, being held in London, are between the GMB and Transport and General Workers' unions (T&G) and the Construction Confederation representing the industry.
A spokesman for the building employers group was not immediately available for comment.
The dispute with the building employers group flared up after the Confederation in May withdrew a three-year pay deal, which the unions rejected as unrealistic.
"The employers failed to make a pay offer (in May) so our members were facing a pay freeze and the talks broke down," a GMB spokeswoman said.
But the return to the negotiating table appeared to mark a thawing of relations between the two sides, the spokeswoman said in an interview.

"(It is positive) because since May 29 we've been trying to get talks and the employers have refused. But when we announced we would be balloting for a strike the employers offered us talks," she said.
The unions are pushing for either a one- or three-year pay deal from the bosses and an hourly rate of about 6.50 pounds ($10.9) for semi-skilled workers by 1999.
Talks follow a strike ballot of union members last Wednesday and the breakdown of talks at the end of May.
The unions are confident of strong backing for a strike when ballot results are published on July 25.
"We'll hit a spread of key employers and key sites with the object of telling them: "You're going to lose loads of money from the strike, so for God's sake sort it out,"" she said.

The threat of strikes by builders follows industrial relations turbulence at British Airways which has been hit in the last month by disputes with its main cabin crew union and separately, with ground staff.
The strike last week by BA cabin crew union members, which cost the airline tens of millions, was the first major industrial action under the new Labour government.
The left-of-centre Labour party has worked hard to improve its links with business while distancing itself from the unions, its historical paymasters.

Barclays, the UK banking giant, faces the result of a strike ballot by its unions over pay and conditions later this month, with the decision due to be announced on the same day as the builders' ballot. Construction workers have not gone on strike since 1973.
T&G representative George Henderson complained earlier this month of skill shortages in the building sector and that workers were not being offered enough money by management.

If members back industrial action on July 25 an indefinite strike may be called from August 5, aiming to cause maximum disruption to employers, who include Tarmac Plc, Costain Group Plc, John Laing Plc and George Wimpey Plc, the union said.
($ = 0.596 British Pounds)
